core: Because resources are scarce relative to wants, every individual, firm, and society must choose among alternatives
Every choice involves a tradeoff: getting more of one thing means giving up something else

The distinction between a tradeoff (everything you give up in general when you choose) and opportunity cost (specifically the value of the single next-best alternative) — with the depth of opportunity cost handed off to the opportunity-cost sibling topic

The production possibilities frontier (PPF) named lightly as a way to picture society's tradeoffs: with limited resources there is a limit to what can be produced, and moving along the frontier means trading one good for another (depth deferred to opportunity-cost and production siblings)
Rational decision-making as weighing the expected benefits of an option against its costs, including opportunity cost
One concrete example of a tradeoff a person faces
supporting: Scarcity is the cause of the need to choose (named, not owned here)
Productive efficiency: a point on the PPF cannot yield more of one good without less of another, while a point inside the frontier wastes resources
Rational does not mean selfish or infallible; it means choosing based on perceived costs and benefits given available information
outOfScope: Scarcity as a full topic — its causes and the finite factors of production (owned by economics:foundations:scarcity)
Opportunity cost in depth, including how to compute it and the law of increasing opportunity cost (owned by economics:foundations:opportunity-cost)
Marginal analysis and deciding at the margin as a method (owned by economics:foundations:marginal-thinking)
The full mechanics, math, and shape (bowed-out) of the production possibilities frontier and comparative advantage (owned by opportunity-cost and later production topics)
Micro versus macro as a survey distinction, supply and demand, incentives, and consumer choice (their own topics)

claims.claim: Economics is the study of how people make decisions under scarcity, where scarcity means human wants for goods, services, and resources exceed what is available; because wants exceed means, individuals, firms, and societies must choose among alternatives.
Because people must choose, they inevitably face tradeoffs: to obtain more of one thing they desire, they have to give up something else they also desire.
A tradeoff refers in general to what must be given up when a choice is made, whereas opportunity cost is specifically the value of the next-best alternative that is given up when a decision is made.

The production possibilities frontier is a model showing the combinations of two goods a society can produce with its limited resources; because resources are limited, there is a limit to the quantities of goods and services that can be produced, and the downward slope shows that producing more of one good requires producing less of the other.

A point on the production possibilities frontier is productively efficient — it is impossible to produce more of one good without decreasing production of the other — while a point inside the frontier represents unused or wasted resources.

Economists model decision-makers as rational agents who weigh the benefits of an option against its costs, including opportunity cost, and undertake an action when its expected benefit exceeds its cost.
